questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
questions.question: A surgeon approaches the anteromedial surface of the parotid gland while performing a radical parotidectomy. Which of the following structures is related to it?
questions.explanation: The anteromedial surface of the parotid gland is related to the medial pterygoid muscle. The parotid gland is the largest salivary gland. It is usually in the shape of an inverted pyramid and has a superior surface, apex, superficial surface, anteromedial surface, and posteromedial surface. Relations: superior surface - external acoustic meatus and posterior part of temporomandibular joint; apex - posterior belly of digastric and carotid triangle; superficial surface - skin, superficial fascia, greater auricular nerve, parotid lymph nodes, and platysma; anteromedial surface - posteroinferior mandibular ramus, masseter, medial pterygoid, and temporomandibular joint; posteromedial surface - mastoid process, posterior belly of digastric, styloid process, and attached muscles.

questions.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about the parotid gland?

options.text: Parotid nodes lie behind the gland

questions.correctAnswerText: Parotid nodes lie behind the gland
questions.explanation: The parotid nodes lie on the superficial surface of the parotid gland. The false capsule covering the parotid gland is derived from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia. Structures present in the parotid gland from superficial to deep are the facial nerve, retromandibular vein, and external carotid artery. The parotid gland is derived from ectoderm.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
questions.question: A radiologist is performing an ultrasound of the parotid gland in a case of parotid abscess. Which of the following structures will he not visualize within the gland?
questions.explanation: The facial artery is not present within the parotid gland. The gland contains the external carotid artery, which terminates as maxillary and superficial temporal arteries, and the transverse facial artery, a branch of the superficial temporal artery. Sometimes the external carotid artery gives the posterior auricular artery within the gland. Veins include maxillary and superficial temporal veins, which unite to form the retromandibular vein. Nerves include the facial nerve and its branches; parotid lymph nodes are also present.

Nerves include the facial nerve and its branches; parotid lymph nodes are also present.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the location of the otic ganglion?
questions.explanation: The secretomotor fibres from the glossopharyngeal nerve relay through the otic ganglion before supplying the parotid gland. The otic ganglion is medial to the mandibular nerve. Relations: superiorly - foramen ovale; laterally - mandibular nerve; medially - tensor veli palatini; posteriorly - middle meningeal artery. The otic ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion below the foramen ovale. Preganglionic fibres originate in the inferior salivatory nucleus and pass through the lesser petrosal nerve, the continuation of the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve, and relay in the ganglion. Postganglionic fibres pass via communicating branches to the auriculotemporal nerve and supply the parotid gland.

questions.question: Match the following with the structures they supply.
questions.explanation: The otic ganglion supplies the parotid gland. The pterygopalatine ganglion (Meckel's ganglion) supplies the lacrimal glands and palatal glands. The submandibular ganglion supplies the submandibular and sublingual glands.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
questions.question: Where does the nerve passing through the marked foramen derive its parasympathetic preganglionic fibres from?
questions.explanation: The image shows the foramen ovale. The lesser petrosal nerve passes through this foramen. It derives preganglionic fibres from the tympanic nerve, also known as Jacobson's nerve. The parasympathetic pathway is: inferior salivatory nucleus → glossopharyngeal nerve (tympanic nerve) → tympanic plexus → lesser petrosal nerve → foramen ovale → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve → parotid gland. The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve also passes through the foramen ovale, but it does not have parasympathetic preganglionic fibres.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
questions.question: A medical student skipped breakfast to attend his morning class. He is currently thinking about having food and coffee after class, and notices increased salivary secretion. The nerve fibres to the parotid gland responsible for this come from all except:
questions.explanation: The case is suggestive of parasympathetic stimulation of the salivary glands, causing increased salivary secretion. Parasympathetic fibres to the parotid gland are carried by the lesser petrosal nerve. Preganglionic fibres originate in the inferior salivatory nucleus, travel via the glossopharyngeal nerve and tympanic plexus into the lesser petrosal nerve, and relay in the otic ganglion. Postganglionic fibres travel through communicating branches to the auriculotemporal nerve and supply the parotid gland. The greater petrosal nerve carries secretomotor fibres to the pterygopalatine ganglion and supplies lacrimal, nasal, and palatine glands. Sympathetic supply to the parotid comes from the plexus around the middle meningeal artery. Sensory supply to the gland is via the auriculotemporal nerve, and to the capsule via the greater auricular nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
questions.question: While performing a parotid sialography, what anatomical landmark would you use to locate the Stensen's duct?
questions.explanation: The parotid duct or Stensen's duct opens opposite the 2nd upper molar tooth. It pierces the buccinator at the level of the 3rd upper molar tooth. Structures pierced by the parotid duct are buccal pad of fat, buccopharyngeal fascia, buccinator muscle, and mucous membrane. Clinically, sialolithiasis is more common in the submandibular gland than the parotid. Parotid duct stones are usually radiolucent and rarely visible on plain radiography; contrast is given during sialography to visualize stones.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
questions.question: Where is the accessory parotid gland present?

options.text: Between the parotid duct and mandible
Below the apex of the parotid gland
Between the parotid duct and zygomatic arch

questions.correctAnswerText: Between the parotid duct and zygomatic arch
questions.explanation: The accessory parotid gland is present between the parotid duct and zygomatic arch. It is usually a detached part of the parotid gland, with its own blood supply and a secondary duct draining into the main parotid duct. It can be missed during complete parotidectomy, can present as mid-cheek masses, and its histological characteristics can differ from the main gland, so tumors may show a different clinical course.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
questions.question: A patient with Frey's syndrome receives a Botox injection into the skin over the parotid region. Which of the following nerves has undergone aberrant innervation in this condition?
questions.explanation: Frey's syndrome occurs due to aberrant innervation of the auriculotemporal nerve and is also known as gustatory sweating or auriculotemporal syndrome. It commonly develops after parotid surgery or trauma with injury to the parotid capsule. During regrowth, an aberrant connection develops between parasympathetic fibres supplying the parotid gland (auriculotemporal nerve) and sweat glands. This causes sweating, warmth, and redness of the face during salivary stimulation by smell or taste of food. Management includes antiperspirants (aluminum chloride), tympanic neurectomy, and botulinum toxin injection into affected skin.

questions.question: Lobes of the structure marked X are divided by ____
questions.explanation: The structure marked X is the submandibular gland. Lobes of the submandibular gland are divided by the mylohyoid muscle. The gland has a larger superficial and smaller deep part separated by mylohyoid; they are continuous around the posterior border of mylohyoid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
questions.question: Which of the following nerves is susceptible to injury in a patient undergoing a submandibular gland excision?
questions.explanation: The lingual nerve is susceptible to injury during excision of the submandibular gland. It loops around the submandibular duct and is therefore vulnerable during procedures in this region. Superficial to hyoglossus, the submandibular duct lies between lingual and hypoglossal nerves. As the duct reaches the anterior border of hyoglossus, it is crossed by the lingual nerve.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man presents with the following finding and is diagnosed with sialadenitis secondary to sialolithiasis. The stone is lodged deep within the gland, hence excision is planned. Which of the following is correct about the surgical anatomy?

options.text: The submandibular gland is seen to wrap around the posterior border of mylohyoid
Facial artery is related to the deep part of the gland
The hypoglossal nerve loops under the submandibular duct
Damage to the lingual nerve will cause loss of sensation to the posterior 1/3rd of the tongue

questions.correctAnswerText: The submandibular gland is seen to wrap around the posterior border of mylohyoid
questions.explanation: The swelling is in the submandibular region and involves the submandibular gland. The gland wraps around the posterior border of the mylohyoid. It has larger superficial and smaller deep parts continuous around this posterior border. The facial artery is related to the superficial part of the gland. The lingual nerve loops around the submandibular duct, and damage to it causes loss of sensation in the anterior 2/3rd of the tongue.
questions.structuredExplanationText: The swelling is in the submandibular region and involves the submandibular gland. The gland wraps around the posterior border of the mylohyoid. questions.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
questions.question: Where do the preganglionic fibers to the submandibular ganglion arise from?
questions.explanation: Preganglionic fibres to the submandibular ganglion arise from the superior salivatory nucleus. The secretomotor pathway is superior salivatory nucleus → facial nerve → chorda tympani → lingual nerve → submandibular ganglion (relay) → postganglionic fibres → submandibular and sublingual glands.

questions.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
questions.question: What does the area marked X overlie?
questions.explanation: The structure marked X is the isthmus of the thyroid gland. It overlies the 2nd, 3rd and 4th tracheal rings. The isthmus connects the lower parts of both lobes and is usually anterior to the 2nd and 3rd tracheal cartilages, though its position may vary with size.

questions.question: You are an intern, scrubbed in on a thyroidectomy. You observe that the operating surgeon ligates the inferior thyroid artery close to the gland. This is done to prevent injury to which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is related to the posterior branch of the inferior thyroid artery near the thyroid lobes. Therefore the artery is ligated close to the gland to prevent nerve injury. The external laryngeal nerve is related to the superior thyroid artery; the superior thyroid artery is also ligated close to the gland to avoid injury to that nerve.

questions.question: Inferior thyroid artery is a branch of ____
questions.explanation: Inferior thyroid artery is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
questions.question: A 62-year-old woman underwent a thyroidectomy for a multinodular goiter. After coming out of anesthesia, the patient reports weakness of the right side of the body and is unable to speak. CT-brain showed multiple scattered air bubbles in the left hemisphere. Intraoperative injury to which of the following structures can lead to this condition?
questions.explanation: The scenario is suggestive of cerebral air embolism. Intra-operative injury to the superior or middle thyroid veins can allow air to be sucked in because of negative venous pressure. The embolus travels via the internal jugular vein into cerebral venous circulation. Head-down position during surgery prevents air embolism. Superior and middle thyroid veins drain into the internal jugular vein; the inferior thyroid vein drains into the brachiocephalic vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
questions.question: You are examining a case of goitre and observe that it moves with deglutition. The movement occurs due to the attachment of the thyroid gland by Berry's ligament, to which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: Movement of the thyroid gland with deglutition is due to the attachment of Berry's ligament to the cricoid cartilage. The pretracheal fascia forms the false capsule and thickens posterolaterally as Berry's (lateral thyroid) ligament, attaching the posteromedial thyroid lobes to the side of the cricoid cartilage. It also prevents the thyroid from sinking into the mediastinum.

questions.question: A 28-year-old male was rushed to the ER after a road traffic accident. He has extensive trauma to the neck, and an emergency mid-line tracheostomy was performed. All of the following structures are prone to injury except:
questions.explanation: The inferior thyroid artery is not damaged during emergency midline tracheostomy because it is not a midline structure. The thyroid isthmus, arteria thyroid ima, and inferior thyroid vein are in the midline and are prone to injury.

questions.question: A 40-year-old female underwent total thyroidectomy and on the third postoperative day complains of numbness in her fingers and perioral area. Which of the following vessels would have been injured during the surgery?

options.text: Anterior branch of superior thyroid artery
Posterior branch of superior thyroid artery
Superior branch of inferior thyroid artery
Inferior branch of inferior thyroid artery

questions.correctAnswerText: Superior branch of inferior thyroid artery
questions.explanation: The scenario suggests postoperative hypoparathyroidism due to injury to the superior branch of the inferior thyroid artery. Parathyroid glands are small yellowish-brown structures between the posterior border of the thyroid gland and its capsule. There are two superior and two inferior glands. They are supplied by the superior branch of the inferior thyroid artery and secrete parathormone.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
questions.question: Which of the following structures prevents the upward extension of thyroid swelling through its attachment to the thyroid cartilage?
questions.explanation: Sternothyroid and sternohyoid prevent upward extension of thyroid swelling through attachment to the thyroid cartilage. Pretracheal fascia encloses the thyroid and attaches to the larynx, producing movement with deglutition. The thyrohyoid membrane is fibro-elastic, arising from the superior margin of thyroid cartilage and attaching to hyoid bone, facilitating upward laryngeal movement during swallowing. Berry's ligament extends from cricoid cartilage to thyroid and prevents the gland from sinking into the mediastinum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Glands of the Head and Neck
questions.question: The newly discovered salivary glands are predominantly present over
questions.explanation: The newly discovered salivary glands are predominantly present over the torus tubarius, the anatomical structure formed by cartilage supporting the entrance of the auditory tube. The proposed name is tubarial salivary glands. They extend caudally to the pharyngeal wall and cranially to Rosenmuller's fossa. PSMA PET/CT can visualize these glands with high sensitivity and specificity. Radiotherapy over their location has been reported to cause xerostomia and dysphagia; sparing them might improve quality of life.
